content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises that individuals who are pregnant should continue their malaria treatment, such as chloroquine, throughout the duration of pregnancy until delivery. This is to prevent potential harm to the unborn baby, such as hemolytic anemia. After delivery, treatment with primaquine may be completed. It is currently unknown whether primaquine passes into breast milk. Before breastfeeding, your infant should be tested for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency by a healthcare provider. Drug interactions can alter the effectiveness of your medications or increase the risk of serious side effects. It is important to maintain a list of all products you use, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, and herbal supplements, and share this information with your doctor and pharmacist. This document does not include all possible drug interactions. In the event of an overdose, if the individual has serious symptoms such as loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, call 911 immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222, and Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669. Laboratory and medical tests, such as G6PD blood tests and blood cell counts, should be conducted before starting this medication and periodically during treatment. It is essential to attend all scheduled medical and laboratory appointments. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is close to the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular dosing schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store this medication at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. This information is a summary and does not contain all possible details about this product. It does not guarantee that the product is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. It is not a substitute for professional medical advice. Always consult your healthcare provider for complete information about this product and your specific health needs. Side effects such as nausea, vomiting, dizziness, stomach upset, and abdominal cramps may occur. Remember that this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks. Serious allergic reactions to this drug are rare. If you experience side effects, contact your doctor for medical advice. Before taking primaquine, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it or have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. Primaquine may cause dizziness, and consuming alcohol or marijuana (cannabis) can worsen this effect. Avoid driving, operating machinery, or performing tasks requiring alertness until you can do so safely. Limit alcoholic beverages. Primaquine may cause a condition affecting heart rhythm (QT prolongation). The risk of QT prolongation may increase if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other drugs that can cause QT prolongation. Low levels of potassium or magnesium in the blood may also increase this risk, which can occur with the use of certain medications (e.g., diuretics or water pills) or conditions such as severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. This medication must not be used during pregnancy, as it may harm an unborn baby. Women of childbearing age should undergo a pregnancy test before starting this medication. It is crucial to prevent pregnancy during and after treatment with primaquine. Both men and women must use reliable forms of birth control, such as condoms or birth control pills, during treatment. Men should continue using birth control for at least three months after completing treatment, while women should continue for at least one menstrual cycle after treatment ends. If you become pregnant or suspect you may be pregnant, inform your doctor immediately. Traveling to areas with malaria during pregnancy significantly increases the risk of death and other complications for both the mother and the infant. The CDC recommends continuing other malaria treatments, such as chloroquine, throughout pregnancy to prevent harm to the unborn baby, including hemolytic anemia. After delivery, primaquine treatment may be completed. It is unknown if this drug passes into breast milk, so your infant should be tested for G6PD deficiency before breastfeeding.
